title: Breaking It on Purpose: Injected Sensor Faults and the Monitor That Has to Notice Each

questions.question: Why break a simulated sensor on purpose?
options: The code that handles a real fault is the most important and least often run, since the real fault happens once a year: a simulator is the only place to run it daily
questions.explanation: The fault is switched on at a chosen time by a line of a scenario.

questions.question: A stuck sensor froze at the last good reading, 2.0. What does it read when the truth is 3.0, and then 9.0?
options: 2.0 and 2.0: it repeats the last good reading
questions.explanation: Readings before the fault are untouched.

questions.question: What is a residual?
options: The difference between the sensor and what a model says it should read, near zero when all is well
questions.explanation: Here a shadow of the motor driven by the same commands.

questions.question: A spike of 0.4 on one reading in 25 was never caught by a monitor needing three in a row. Why is that not a bug?
options: One reading is not a run: the monitor was built to ignore a single reading, and whether a lone spike matters is for a different monitor, such as a Hampel filter
questions.explanation: The offset was caught in 0.02 s, the drift in 0.46.

questions.question: A stuck sensor at the target was caught by the residual monitor 2.85 s late and by the stuck monitor at the move. Why?
options: A frozen reading at the target looks right and the loop commands almost nothing, so the residual stays small; the stuck monitor knows an unchanging reading is wrong only when motion was expected
questions.explanation: Each monitor sees what the other cannot.

questions.question: What did raising the residual threshold from 0.02 to 0.2 cost, against a drift of 0.05 a second?
options: The drift was found 4.04 s after it began instead of 0.46: nine times later, with the position by then wrong by 0.2
questions.explanation: Set low it gave false alarms: 200 of 200 runs at twice the noise.
